title: There's a GALAXY in Your Sky Wider Than the Moon 🌌
description:
There's a galaxy in your sky six times wider than the Moon. Never seen it? Your eyes are just really bad at dim: they grab light for a blink, while a camera grabs it for minutes... and then the rest of the Andromeda galaxy shows up, nearly six full Moons long. And that glow left it about two and a half million years ago, before people like us existed. Sorry, Moon.
Have you ever seen it? Yes or no?

The science: in long-exposure photos the Andromeda galaxy (M31) spans about 3 degrees of sky, nearly six full Moons end to end (the full Moon is about half a degree wide): NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day (21 Oct 2022, 21 Feb 2025) and the M31 entry in Wikipedia (3.17 by 1 degrees). With your eyes alone, even on a dark night, you mostly see its bright middle as a faint smudge: your eye builds each picture over roughly a tenth of a second, while a camera can keep collecting light for seconds or minutes (the Moon in this Short is drawn at the same scale, the way a long-exposure photo sees it). Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light you see left it about 2.5 million years ago; our own species is about 300,000 years old (Hublin et al., Nature 2017).
